Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 61, verse 1:

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾

Page 174

The connection of this opening to what follows in the surah: it explains that the disbelievers deserve to be fought by you, because they have deviated from all of creation. They do not glorify Allah, and they do not ascribe to Him the attributes of perfection, since they have made partners with Him in divinity. There is also an allusion (ta'rid) to those who failed to keep what they promised, namely that they did not render Allah His due of glorification. This is because Allah deserves to have His covenant fulfilled in this worldly life, and because Allah is the helper of those who believe against their enemy.

The discussion of the like of His saying (sabbaha lillah) up to (al-Hakim) has already been presented at the beginning of Surat al-Hashr and Surat al-Hadid.

In the use of the attribute (al-'Aziz) for Him, exalted is He, here, there is an indication (ima') that He is the one who overcomes His enemy. Therefore it was not fitting for you to fear His enemies so that you flee from them at the time of encounter.

As for the use of the attribute (al-Hakim): if it is taken to mean the one characterized by wisdom, then the one characterized by wisdom does not command you to fight the enemy in vain, nor does He leave them to overcome you. And if it is taken to mean the one who makes affairs firm (al-muhkim lil-umur), then it is likewise.

[Page 175]

He addressed them by the description of faith, as an allusion that faith is of such a nature that it restrains the believer from letting his deeds contradict his words regarding a promise of good.

The lam (ل) expresses the cause of the thing being asked about, which is the unspecified matter that is the referent of the interrogative *mā* (ما), because it indicates an unspecified matter whose specification is sought.

The implied meaning is: "You say what you do not do, for what reason or for what cause?"

The lam is connected to the verb *taqūlūna* (تَقُولُونَ), and the interrogative particle, having precedence in the sentence, is placed before the preposition and its object.

The question about the cause is used here to deny that the reason for this be pleasing to God the Exalted, that is, what prompts them to this is a reprehensible matter. This is a kināya (metonymy, an indirect expression) for blame and warning against it, as in the words of God the Exalted, ﴿Say: Why then did you kill the prophets of God before?﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:91), in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 176]

Accordingly, the statement they made may have been a promise that they gave and did not fulfil. It may also have been a report they gave about themselves that did not correspond to reality. The full treatment of this has already been given in the discussion of the beginning of the surah.

This is a kināya for warning them against falling into the like of what they did on the day of Uhud, by way of indirect allusion, and a kināya for blame for what they did on the day of Uhud, by way of hinting.

The verse is followed by the words ﴿Indeed, God loves those who fight in His cause in a battle line, as if they were a solid structure﴾ (Al-Saff 61:4), etc., which indicates that the blame for a promise concerns striving in the cause of God. In this way the meaning of the verse harmonizes with the hadith of al-Tirmidhi regarding the occasion of revelation, and other narrations that were related about its occasion, which he mentioned in al-Kashshaf, are refuted.

In it there is also an allusion to the hypocrites, since they profess faith with their words while not doing the deeds of the people of faith, neither with the heart nor with the body. Ibn Zayd said: "It is the saying of the hypocrites to the believers: 'We are with you and of you,' and then their actions show the opposite of that."

The clause ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of God that you say what you do not do﴾ is an explanation of the clause ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾, making explicit the meaning that was expressed indirectly by it.

It is a statement that their saying ﴿what you do not do﴾ is a great matter within the category of hatred.

Kibar (كِبَرُ, greatness) is used metaphorically for intensity, because the great thing in its kind has abundance and intensity.

*An taqūlū* (أنْ تَقُولُوا) is the subject (fā'il) of *kabura* (كَبُرَ).

Al-maqt (المَقْتُ) is intense hatred, and here it has the meaning of the passive participle.

*Maqtan* (مَقْتًا) is in the accusative as a tamyīz (specification, an accusative of specification) of the respect in which the greatness applies. It is a tamyīz of attribution.

The implied meaning is: "Your saying what you do not do is greatly hateful."

This statement is composed first in a general form and then in a detailed form by means of the tamyīz, to magnify this matter in the hearts of the listeners, because many of them are prone to negligence in guarding against it, to the point that they fell into what they fell into on the day of Uhud. Therefore it contains a threat against the recurrence of the like of it. The intended meaning was further emphasized by describing the hatred as being "in the sight of God," meaning a hatred that admits no leniency.

[Page 176 continued]

He departed from making the subject of *kabura* a pronoun referring to the saying, by restricting it to ﴿greatly hateful in the sight of God﴾, or by saying "that is greatly hateful," in order to intensify the magnification by repeating the expression and to add emphasis.

The *mā* (ما) in His words "*mā lā taf'alūna*" (ما لا تَفْعَلُونَ) in both places is a relative pronoun, and it has the meaning of the definite lam (lam al-'ahd, the definite article of prior reference), meaning: the act that you promised to do, and that is the most beloved of deeds to God, or striving (al-jihād). The verse therefore requires that a promise of this kind must be fulfilled, because what is promised is an act of obedience, and so a promise to do it is of the nature of a vow (nadhr) whose purpose is nearness to God, and thus its fulfilment is obligatory.

Al-ṣaff (the battle line, or row): a number of things standing side by side in an ordered arrangement. It is applied to the rows of worshippers, the rows of the angels, and the rows of an army on the battlefield. When the army is present for battle, it forms a line of infantry or cavalry, and then some advance toward others, individually or in groups.

Thus al-ṣaff here is a kināya (an allusive or metonymic expression) for organization and for fighting with deliberate planning.

As for the movements of combat, they occur according to the requirements of war: gathering and dispersal, attack and retreat. The word ﴿صَفًّا﴾ is in the accusative as a ḥāl (a circumstantial state, an adverbial accusative), with the sense of "lined up" (ṣāffīna) or "arranged in rows" (maṣfūfīna).

Al-marṣūṣ: tightly joined, one part adjoining another. The simile is in steadfastness and in not breaking ranks. This is what the earlier rebuke required, in His words ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Ṣaff: 2].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 61, verse 5:

﴿And [remember] when Moses said to his people: "O my people, why do you harm me, when you know that I am the Messenger of Allah to you?" So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾

Page 177

The placement of this verse here has an obscure connection. It may be that the sentence is an independent parenthetical (i'tiraD) introduced as a fresh beginning (isti'naf ibtida'i), by which the discourse moves from the prohibition against failing to fulfil what they promised Allah to a allusion (ta'rid) to a people who harmed the Prophet ﷺ by speech, by disobedience, or the like. In that case the speech is directed at the hypocrites, for they were branded with harming the Messenger ﷺ. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger – Allah has cursed them in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 57], and ﴿And those who harm the Messenger of Allah – for them is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Tawbah: 61], and His saying: "And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, 'He is an ear.'"

On this interpretation, it is a transition (iqtiḍab) by which the discourse passes from the previous theme, having been completed, to this theme. Or the reason for its placement in this position may be that a cause arose that required its revelation, namely some harm that occurred which the exegetes and the transmitters of reports and occasions of revelation (asbab al-nuzul) did not come to know.

On this view, the waw (and) is the conjunction of one theme to another; this is what is called the conjunction of one narrative to another narrative (ʿatf qiṣṣa ʿalā qiṣṣa).

It is also possible that it is a continuation of the preceding speech: Allah struck an example for the Muslims to warn them against doing what harms His Messenger ﷺ and grieves him, such as the deviation from the path of religious perfection, like failing to fulfil their promise to perform the most beloved deeds to Allah the Exalted. And [the verse] is most solicitous that this may be a cause of deviation and misguidance, as occurred to the people of Moses when they harmed him.

On this interpretation, the harm of the people of Moses to him means: their failure to seek his obedience and pleasure. This points to what Allah related of his saying: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has assigned to you, and do not turn back on your heels, lest you turn about as losers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21], up to His saying: ﴿They said, "O Moses, indeed we will never enter it as long as they are in it. So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we are sitting right here."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]. Their saying that is contempt, and what supports this is His saying after it: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I control none except myself and my brother, so separate us from the defiantly disobedient people."﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 25].

It may also be that their description in this verse, ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾, refers to their being described thus twice in the surah of al-Ma'idah, in His saying: ﴿So separate us from the defiantly disobedient people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 25] and His saying: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 26].

Page 178

Thus the most important purpose of the story is what branches from its mention, namely His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate.﴾ It is appropriate that this verse be a warning against opposing the command of the Messenger ﷺ, and a lesson from the defeat that befell them on the day of Uhud when they opposed his command by not remaining steadfast in their positions as archers.

The two stories resemble each other in that the people fled on the day of Uhud just as the people of Moses fled on the day of Jericho (Ariha), and in that the archers whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had ordered not to leave their place ("even if the birds snatch us away") and to shoot arrows to cover the army lest the enemy come upon it from behind did not do what he commanded them, and disobeyed the order of their commander ʿAbd Allah ibn Jubayr, and left their station seeking booty. That was the cause of the defeat of the Muslims on the day of Uhud.

On this interpretation, the waw is the conjunction of a warning derived from His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾ onto the prohibition in His saying: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2], and so on.

Following this is the consolation of the Messenger ﷺ for what occurred from the disobedience of the archers, to the extent that they caused the defeat of the people.

The particle (idh) is connected to a verb omitted, whose estimate is: "Remember." It has many parallels in the Qur'an, i.e., remember also for them the time of Moses' saying to his people, or remember for them along with this prohibition the time of Moses' saying to his people.

The beginning of Moses' speech, peace be upon him, with "O my people" is an allusion that the proper condition of the people of a Messenger is to obey him, let alone to harm him. Thus, in the address with the description "people" there is a preparation for the rebuke in his saying: "Why do you harm me?"

The interrogative is for denial, i.e., denying that there should be any cause for harm, as already mentioned in His saying: ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2].

The clause of the circumstantial phrase following His saying: ﴿and you know that I am the Messenger of Allah﴾ came in a fitting position of escalation in the denial.

The (min) here serves to affirm the circumstantial sense, i.e., your knowledge of my message from Allah is a certainty, given what they witnessed of the signs of his message. And just as their knowledge was emphasized by (qad), the attainment of the known was emphasized by (anna) with the fatha, so two emphases were given to the messengership. The meaning: how then does your affair not proceed in accordance with this knowledge?

Page 179

The use of the present tense after (qad) here indicates that their knowledge of this is renewed with the renewal of the signs and revelation, and this is more beneficial for the continuance of their compliance, for if the past tense had been used it would indicate no more than that this knowledge had been attained in the past. Perhaps something has since occurred that nullifies it. This is like the present tense in His saying: ﴿Allah already knows those among you who hinder others﴾ [al-Ahzab: 18] in the surah of al-Ahzab.

Zaygh is deviation from the truth: that is, when they opposed what their Messenger had commanded them, Allah placed deviation in their hearts, i.e., deviation took firm hold of their souls, so they did not part from misguidance.

The sentence ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil): that is, this is Allah's custom among people, and the people of Moses who harmed him were among the people of that generality.

The description "defiantly disobedient" (fasiqin) is mentioned following the word "people" (qawm) to indicate the depravity (fusuq) that became part of the constituents of their peoplehood, as was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164] up to His saying: ﴿are signs for a people who reason﴾ in al-Baqarah.

So the meaning: those for whom deviation from the truth was a disposition do not receive Allah's gentle favour nor does He care for them with a special care that would guide them to right guidance; rather, they are subject to causes and circumstances.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 61, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Children of Israel, indeed I am the messenger of Allah to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah and giving glad tidings of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad." But when he came to them with clear evidences, they said, "This is obvious magic."﴾

This is an conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And when Moses said to his people﴾ [al-Saff: 5]. So according to the first view regarding the position of the preceding statement, the position of this one is equivalent to it.

As for the second view regarding the previous verse, this one is brought as a complement to the story of Moses, by way of mentioning another example of a people who deviated from obedience to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent to them, without conveying a warning to the Muslim addressees, and as a transition to mentioning the reports about Jesus and the Messenger who comes after him.

Jesus addressed his people with the title "Children of Israel" rather than "O my people" because after Moses the Children of Israel became known by the title "Children of Israel," and the title "the people of Moses" was not applied to them except during the lifetime of Moses specifically, for they became a nation and a people only through him and his law.

As for Jesus, he was sent to confirm the law of Moses, to remind them of it, and to change some of its rulings. Moreover, when Jesus addressed them they had not yet followed him or believed him, so they were not a people belonging to him exclusively.

The discussion of the meaning of ﴿confirming what came before me of the Torah﴾ has already been presented at the beginning of Surat Al ʿImran and in the course of Surat al-ʿUqud.

The purpose of drawing their attention to this confirmation when he began the call was to bring about their acceptance and to draw down their inclination, because of their strong adherence to the Torah and their belief that its rulings do not accept abrogation and that they are permanent. For this reason, when he began with this call, he did not add to it what is related from him in Surat Al ʿImran, his saying ﴿and to make lawful for you some of that which was forbidden to you﴾ [Al ʿImran: 50]. That statement is to be understood as a address occurring after the initial call, for Allah did not reveal to him at first the abrogation of some rulings of the Torah and then reveal it to him afterward. Then, at that time, he informed them of what had been revealed to him.

Likewise, the nature of legislation is that it is delivered to the community gradually, as in the Hadith of 'A'isha in Sahih al-Bukhari, that she said: "What was first revealed of it (i.e., the Qur'an) was a surah from the Mufassal in which there is mention of Paradise and Hell, until when people turned to Islam, the lawful and the unlawful were revealed. Had the first thing revealed been, 'Do not drink wine,' they would have said, 'We will never abandon wine,' and had it been, 'Do not commit adultery,' they would have said, 'We will never abandon fornication.' Indeed, it was revealed at Mecca to Muhammad ﷺ while I was a young girl playing: ﴿Rather, the Hour is their appointed time, and the Hour is more calamitous and more bitter﴾ [al-Qamar: 46]. The surahs al-Baqarah and al-Nisa' were not revealed except while I was with him." End of quote.

So the meaning of his saying ﴿confirming what came before me of the Torah﴾ in both verses is confirmation in the sense of affirming and acting upon it in general, that is, acting upon its totality and the bulk of its rulings. This does not contradict the fact that some of its rulings were changed by revelation from Allah in a few circumstances.

Tabshir (glad tidings) is the informing of an event that pleases; here it is applied to the informing of a matter of great benefit to them, because true joy necessarily follows from it, for the coming of a Messenger to people is a great blessing.

The reason for choosing this expression is the allusion to what occurred in the Gospel describing the message of the promised Messenger as "the glad tidings of the kingdom" (bishārat al-malakūt).

He informed them of the coming of a messenger after him because the Children of Israel had always been waiting for the coming of a messenger from Allah who would deliver them from the grip of those who dominated them, and this waiting was their habit. They had been promised this deliverer through the tongues of their prophets after Moses. So Jesus' promise of him was like the promise of those prophets before him, and he opened with it at the beginning of the call, out of concern for this charge.

In beginning with it there is an indication that Jesus is not the awaited deliverer, and that the one awaited is a messenger who comes after him, namely Muhammad ﷺ.

Because of the great standing of this promised Messenger, Allah willed to establish for the nations in which he would appear signs and indications by which they might identify his person, so that their fulfillment would be an opening to their turning toward receiving his call. Those who truly know them fully are the firmly grounded in knowledge among the People of the Book, for they are the ones to whom the common folk of their religion refer. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize him as they recognize their own sons. But indeed, a party of them conceal the truth while they know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. And He said: ﴿Say: "Sufficient is Allah as a witness between me and you, and whoever has knowledge of the Book"﴾ [al-Ra'd: 43].

Allah described some attributes of this Messenger to Moses, peace be upon him, in His saying, relating His response to Moses' supplication: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things, so I will prescribe it for those who fear Me﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], up to His saying ﴿those who follow the Messenger, the unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, who enjoins upon them what is right and forbids them what is wrong, makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the evil things, and relieves them of their burden and the shackles that were upon them﴾ [al-A'raf: 157].

When Allah the Exalted willed to prepare mankind to accept the message of this great Messenger promised, peace and blessings be upon him, He deposited his signs and indications through the tongue of every messenger He sent to people. Allah the Exalted said: "﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: 'Whatever I have given you of Scripture and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him.' He said, 'Do you affirm and accept My commitment on that?' They said, 'We affirm it.' He said, 'Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses.'﴾ [Al ʿImran: 81] ﴿Whoever turns away after that, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al ʿImran: 82]" — that is, did you take My commitment from your nations to believe in the Messenger who comes confirming the messengers? And His saying "bear witness" means, over your nations. What will come from the narration of Jesus' speech in the Gospel will explain this testimony.

Allah the Exalted also said, concerning what He taught Abraham, peace be upon him: ﴿Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom﴾ [al-Baqarah: 129], and so on.

Jesus, peace be upon him, bequeathed in this verse a comprehensive charge that gathers the charges of the prophets before him, summarizing it in a symbolic manner. This is a method of the people of wisdom and prophethood when not explaining the law. Al-Suhrawardi said in Hikmat al-Ishraq: "The words of the Ancients are symbolic." Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi said in his commentary: "They used symbols in their speech, either to sharpen the mind through exercising thought, or in imitation of the Creator, the Exalted, and the possessors of laws in what they brought of revealed symbolic books, so that it would be closer to the understanding of the masses; the elite would benefit from its inner meaning and the common people from its outer meaning." End of quote. That is, so that the people of knowledge among the People of the Book might discern it, and from the totality of its details the characteristics of the promised Messenger would be gathered for them, and it would not be confused for them with someone else who claims that falsely, or whom a group of people falsely or mistakenly claims for him.

The phrase "whose name is Ahmad" should not be understood according to what is immediately suggested by the word "name" (ism), namely a proper name that is unknown, used to indicate a specific entity in order to distinguish it from others who do not share that name, because this understanding is precluded, and because it does not correspond to reality: the promised Messenger was not called Ahmad by people, so no one called the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ by the name Ahmad, neither before his prophethood nor after it, and this is not known.

As for what occurs in the Muwatta' and the Two Sahihs from Muhammad ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "I have five names: I am Muhammad, I am Ahmad, I am al-Mahi (the Eraser) through whom Allah erases disbelief, I am al-Hashir (the Gatherer) at whose feet people will be gathered, and I am al-'Aqib (the Last)." Its interpretation is that he applied the term "names" to what includes the proper name and the characteristic description specific to him, by way of generalization. Other names beyond these have also been transmitted, which Abu Bakr Ibn al-'Arabi listed exhaustively in al-'Arida and al-Qabas.

So what we are certain of is that the meaning of his saying "whose name is Ahmad" applies to all that the two parts of this sentence carry of meanings.

As for the word "ism" (name), its most common usage in Arabic speech is in three uses. The first: that it means the named (al-musammā). Abu 'Ubayda said: "The ism is the musammā." Tha'lab attributed to Sibawayh that the ism is other than the musammā (that is, when the word ism is used in speech, what is meant by it is the named thing of that name). However, Ibn al-Sayyid al-Batalyawsi decided, in his book which he devoted to the meanings of "ism: is it the same as the musammā?", that it occurs in some places in Sibawayh's book that the ism is the musammā, and in others that it is other than the musammā; Ibn al-Sayyid al-Batalyawsi interpreted this as two usages, not a contradiction in Sibawayh's words. Tha'lab hesitated on this and said: "I have no opinion on it." And because of the possibility of ambiguity in this usage, its use as proof has been invalidated.

The second usage: that ism means fame for goodness. Tha'lab recited:

"For the greatest of them in rank, the noblest of them in lineage, the most handsome of them in face, and the most widely proclaimed in renown."

Sama is a dialectal form of ism.

The third usage: that it is applied to a word established to indicate an entity so that it may be distinguished from many of its like; this is the proper name (ʿalam).

We proceed according to our principle of interpreting the words of the Qur'an in all the meanings that correct usage permits, as in the ninth introduction of this tafsir. Accordingly, we understand the ism in his saying "his name is Ahmad" as encompassing all three of these usages together: that is, its named (musammā) is Ahmad, its mention is Ahmad, and its proper name is Ahmad. Let us understand the word Ahmad in a way that is not rejected by any of the usages of the word ism when combined with it, namely that Ahmad is a comparative form (ism tafdil) which may be stripped of the sense of comparison, meaning the intensity of that from which it is derived, namely hamd (praise), which is commendation. So Ahmad here is used in the sense of the passive participle of praise, that is, people's praise of him, as in their saying "al-'ud ahmad" (the wood is most praiseworthy), meaning greatly praised. The description by "Ahmad," with respect to the first meaning of ism, is that the named of this Messenger, and his very person, is described by the most excellent thing for which a praiseworthy one is praised; this includes all the perfections of soul, character, physical form, lineage, people, and other things that are counted among essential and purposive perfections.

It is also valid to take "Ahmad" as a true comparative in the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, that is, his named is more praiseworthy than me, i.e., more excellent, i.e., in his message and law. The expressions of the Gospel indicate this excellence: in the Gospel of John, chapter fourteen: "And I will ask the Father, that is our Lord, and He will give you another Paraclete (faraqlit) to abide with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees Him nor knows Him." Then he said: "But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father (God) will send, He will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you," meaning among what He teaches you, that He will remind you of all that I have said to you. This indicates his superiority over Jesus through the excellence of the permanence of his law, expressed by the Gospel's words "that He may abide with you forever," and through the excellence of the universality of his law for rulings, expressed by his words "He will teach you all things."

The description by "Ahmad" according to the second meaning of ism is that his fame and mention among his generation and the generations after him are described as the most intense praiseworthy mention and praiseworthy renown. This is the meaning of his saying in the hadith: "I am the bearer of the banner of praise on the Day of Resurrection," and that Allah will raise him to a praiseworthy station.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 61, verse 6 (part 2 of 2):

The description "Ahmad" (Aḥmad), in relation to the third meaning of the name, is an indication that his proper name carries the sense of "Ahmad." The word Muhammad is a passive participle (ism maf'ul) of the doubled verb hammada, which indicates the frequency of the praise of those who praise him, just as they say: "So-and-so is mumaddah (much praised)," when his praise has been repeated by many who praise him.

Thus the name Muhammad conveys the meaning "the one who is praised abundantly," and this is alluded to by Ahmad.

This comprehensive word, which God revealed to 'Isa (peace be upon him), God intended to be a emblem gathering the attributes of the promised Messenger (ﷺ). It was formulated in the most excellent form that indicates these attributes in summary, to the extent that language permits the gathering of meanings. Its detailed explanation was left to what appears of his characteristics before and after his mission, so that those who discern (al-mutawassimun) may perceive them and those firmly grounded in knowledge (al-rasikhun) may contemplate their depths upon witnessing and experience.

In the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 24, the words of 'Isa appear: "And many false prophets will arise and will deceive many. But he who endures to the end, he will be saved. And this gospel of the kingdom will be preached in all the world as a witness to all the nations, and then the end will come." The meaning of "yakriz" (preaches) is "calls and announces," and the meaning of "reaches the end" is "delays until near the Hour."

In the Gospel of John, chapter 14: "If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete (farqaliṭ), to abide with you forever." The word "farqalit" is Greek (Rumi), that is, Syriac (Buwaniyya), and is used in the sense of "the defender" or "the comforter," i.e., one who brings that which removes sorrows and calamities, that is, who comes as a mercy, that is, a messenger giving good tidings. The word "another" is explicit that he is a messenger like 'Isa.

In chapter 14 also: "The word that you hear is not mine but his who sent me. I have spoken these things to you while I am still with you" — that is, during my existence among you — "but the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and bring to your remembrance all that I have said." The meaning of "in my name" is "by the attribute of the message." "I will not talk with you much, for the ruler of this world is coming, and he has no power over me. But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father commanded me, so I do."

In chapter 15 of the same: "When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me."

These reports establish that this announced Messenger's message encompasses all nations in all the earth, that he is the Seal, and that his law has dominion, according to the words of Matthew's Gospel: "he will preach the good news of the kingdom" — and "the kingdom" is the king. Also, that his teachings relate to all the matters that befall people; that is, his law's rulings relate to all human circumstances, and all of these are included in the word spoken by 'Isa (peace be upon him), namely the word "his name is Ahmad." Thus it was among the divine symbols, and because it was intended for this purpose, God the Exalted mentioned it in the Qur'an as a reminder and a proclamation.

The Qur'an's mention of 'Isa's good tidings of Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon them both) within the course of its main theme — the comparison of what Musa suffered from his people with what 'Isa suffered from his people — is an incidental addition (idmaj) that strengthens the Prophet (ﷺ), steadies his heart, and increases his consolation. It also contains a transition to the point that what he encountered from his people is similar to what 'Isa encountered from the Children of Israel.

His saying ﴿So when he came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is manifest magic."﴾ is the locus of the harm.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun of nominative (raf') in his saying "jaa'hum" returns to 'Isa, and the pronoun of accusative (nasb) returns to those whom 'Isa addressed. The implied sense: "they denied him; then when he came to them with the miracles, they said, 'This is magic,' or 'he is a magician.'"

It is also possible that the pronoun of nominative refers to a messenger who would come after me, and the pronoun of accusative refers to the phrase "Children of Israel," meaning the Children of Israel other than those whom 'Isa, peace be upon him, called — in the manner of: "I have a dirham and its half," meaning half of what is called a dirham. That is: when the Messenger whom 'Isa called by the name Ahmad came to them with clear proofs, i.e., indications of the applicability of the promised attributes, they said, "This is manifest magic" or "This is a manifest magician." In this case the structure is of the type of "speech directed" (al-kalam al-muwajjah).

Their harm came through this saying to both messengers.

According to this possibility, the sentence is understood as an interjection (i'tiraḍ) between the coordinated clauses (mutaʿatifat), and as a preparation for the transition to censure of the polytheists and others who did not accept the call of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read the yaʾ in his saying "ba'di" (after me) with a fatha. The rest read it with a sukun. Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: "al-Khalil and Sibawayh preferred the fatha."

The majority read "hadha sihr" (this is magic) with a kasra on the sin. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read "hadha sahir" (this is a magician). According to the first reading, the demonstrative refers to the clear proofs (al-bayyinat); according to the second, the demonstrative refers to 'Isa or to the Messenger.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 61, verse 7:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah while he is being invited to Islam? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

The call of the Prophet ﷺ was similar to the call of ʿIsa (peace be upon him), and the response of those whom he invited to Islam from among the People of the Book and the polytheists was similar to the response of those whom ʿIsa (peace be upon him) invited. When [the passage] incorporated, within the narration of ʿIsa's call, his good tidings of a messenger who would come after him, it was fitting to shift the speech to what the people of the promised Messenger responded to their Messenger with. Therefore, in the call of this Messenger, the religion of Islam is mentioned, and they are described as "the most unjust of people," as a condemnation of their state.

Page 188

Thus, what is meant by this interrogative are those who denied the Prophet ﷺ. For this reason, this statement is conjoined with the particle "wa" (and) rather than "fa" (then), because it is not a consequence of the call of ʿIsa (peace be upon him).

This condemnation encompasses all those who denied the call of the Prophet ﷺ from among the People of the Book and the polytheists.

The primary intended group are the People of the Book, and it will come, at the words of the Exalted ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ [al-Saff: 8] up to His words ﴿though the polytheists dislike it﴾ [al-Saff: 9], that they are two groups.

The interrogative with "man aẓlamu" (who is more unjust) is a denial, meaning there is no one more unjust than these; the deniers before them either are more unjust than them, or equal to them in every case. So the statement is hyperbole.

They were the most unjust of people because they wronged the Messenger ﷺ by attributing to him what is not in him, when they said: "He is a sorcerer." They wronged themselves in that they did not seek salvation for themselves, by presenting the Messenger's ﷺ call to sound reflection until they knew its truthfulness. They wronged their Lord in that they ascribed what came to them of His guidance and the proofs of His Messenger ﷺ to what is not from Him, calling the signs and proofs "sorcery." They wronged people by driving them to denial, and they wronged them by concealing the reports that came in the Torah and the Gospel affirming the truthfulness of the Messenger of Islam ﷺ. The words of the Exalted ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ completed this injustice for them, so it is known that it is a continuous injustice.

The clause of circumstance ﴿while he is being invited to Islam﴾ has a firm position here, meaning: they did this while the Messenger was calling them to that in which lies their good, so they exchanged gratitude for disbelief.

Their fabrication of lies against Allah was attributed to them because they denied a Messenger who informs them that he is sent from Allah. The sanctity of this attribution required that they turn to contemplation and reflection on what he called them to, so that they might arrive at belief. When they hastened to turn away from it and ascribed deficiencies to the caller, they had attributed that to Allah without reverence.

As for the People of the Book, they denied the attributes described in their Book, as the Exalted said concerning them: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 140] in Surat al-Baqarah. That is a fabrication.

As for the polytheists, they fabricated against Allah when they said: ﴿Allah has not sent down anything upon a human being﴾ [al-Anʿam: 91].

Page 189

The name "al-Islam" is a proper name for the religion brought by the Prophet ﷺ, which encompasses what holds the good of this world and the Hereafter. So the mention of this name in the circumstantial clause adds to the condemnation of the state of those who turned away from it, meaning: while he is being invited to that in which lies its good. By this, the description "most unjust" is deserved.

The clause ﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a declaration of despair to them of abandoning this injustice, meaning: those who have reached this extent of injustice have no hope for their correction, because disbelief has taken firm hold of them, until it mixed with their natures and became established along with their peoplehood. For this reason, the word "qawm" (people) was inserted to indicate that injustice has reached the point of becoming one of the constituents of their peoplehood, as was mentioned previously in the Exalted's words ﴿Surely in that are signs for a people who reason﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah. And it has been mentioned more than once before.

This encompasses those spoken of and their likes, those who fabricated against ʿIsa; thus it carries the sense of a concluding generalization (tadhyil).

The negation of their guidance is attributed to Allah the Exalted, because the cause of the absence of this guidance from them is one of the effects of the formation of their minds and faculties in obstinacy, through the causal factors that Allah placed in the order of the formation and development of beings, from the connection of effects to their causes; with the caution that Allah does not reach most of them with His care, so He alters in them some of the faculties that prevent them from guidance, out of anger toward them, since they did not sincerely pursue a call worthy of insight by way of its attribution to the side of Allah the Exalted, until truth becomes distinct to them from falsehood and right from wrong.

This is a continuation of the commentary on verse 8 of Surah al-Saff (61). The passage begins mid-argument, as in the original.

Translation:

This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani) arising from the report about them that they fabricated lies against God while they were being invited to Islam, because it raises the question of a questioner about what prompted them to this fabrication. It is answered that they want to extinguish Islam from the people and to hinder its spread. Their condition is likened to the condition of a group who seek darkness for theft or for other things in which concealment is desired.

Then there appears to him the flicker of a lamp's wick shining for people, so they dislike that and fear that its light will spread over the people and their nonsense will be exposed. So they set out to extinguish it by blowing on it, but it did not go out.

The statement is therefore an image (tamthil) indicating the condition of those represented. The sense is: they want to stop the manifestation of Islam, like a people who want to extinguish a light. This is a comparison of form to form, the comparison of the intellectual to the sensory.

Furthermore, among its elegances is that it admits of distributing the comparison over the parts of the form: the Jews, in their wanting to hinder Islam from appearing, are likened to a people who want to extinguish the light of Islam, and so it is likened to a lamp. The polytheists are like them. The condition of the People of the Book has been depicted by a parallel of this image in His words, exalted is He, ﴿And the Jews say, "Ezra is the son of God"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 30], up to His words ﴿They want to extinguish the light of God with their mouths, but God refuses except to perfect His light﴾ [al-Tawbah: 32], the verse in Surah Bara'ah. Their description of the Qur'an as sorcery and similar of their deceptions is likened to the blowing of blowers upon the lamp. So the mention of (with their mouths) has a great effect in this image, because extinguishing may occur by means other than mouths, such as a fan or a bellows, and they wanted to nullify the verses of the Qur'an by claiming that they are among the utterances of sorcery.

The annexation of "light" (nur) to the Name of Majesty (Allah) is an annexation of honour, meaning a light that God kindled, that is, brought into existence and decreed; so consider then His perfection.

The lam in His words (li-yutfi'u) is called the superfluous lam (al-lam al-za'idah), and it gives emphasis. Its origin is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil); the cause of the act of wanting is mentioned in place of its object, by treating the object as if it were the cause.

The sense is: they want to extinguish the light of God, in order that they may extinguish it. This lam frequently occurs after the root of wanting and the root of commanding. Some grammarians of Arabic called it the lam of (an), because the meaning of the verbal (an) is inseparable from it. The discussion of it was given earlier at His words, exalted is He, ﴿God desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26] in Surah al-Nisa'. Therefore it is said that this lam after the verb of wanting is superfluous for emphasis.

The clause ﴿And God perfects His light﴾ is conjoined to the clause (they want), and it is a report that they will not reach their aim and that this religion will be completed, that is, will reach the fullness of spread. In a hadith: "By God, this matter will be completed until a rider travels from San'a to Hadramawt fearing none but God or the wolf for his sheep, but you are hasty."

The nominal sentence indicates the establishment of this completion. Completion (tamam) is the attainment of all that belongs to a thing in quality or quantity; so the completion of light is the attainment of its strongest ray, and its completion is supplying its instrument with what strengthens its ray, such as adding oil to the lamp and removing what covers it.

The clause ﴿though the disbelievers dislike it﴾ is a circumstantial clause, and (law) is the conjunctive law (law al-wasliyyah). It indicates that the content of its condition is the least likely thing to be thought to occur, while the content of the response is occurring alongside it. For this reason the grammarians supply before it what indicates the supposition of the condition's occurrence, saying "this if it were not so, but even if it were so," and this is a supplying of meaning, not an elision, because such an elided element does not apply in every position; it does not fit in His words, exalted is He, ﴿You will not be believed by us even if we were truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 17], since one does not say "if we were liars" but "even if we were truthful." Likewise in this verse, for the meaning is: God perfects His light despite the disbelievers' dislike; and since the disbelievers' dislike of the completion of this light is certain, its context is in the form of a supposed command, as mockery. The use of this (law) was previously discussed at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Never will be accepted from any of them the earth full of gold even if he should ransom himself with it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91] in Surah Al 'Imran.

The disbelievers' dislike of the manifestation of God's light is a state in which the completion of the light is thought to be absent, because that dislike prompts them to band together to create obstacles and to mislead those who seek guidance and turn them away from it by means of deceit, treachery, scheming and harm.

The word "disbelievers" (al-kafirun) includes all who disbelieve in Islam, from among the polytheists, the People of the Book and others.

However, the Qur'anic usage has become established in restricting the description "disbelievers" to the People of the Book and contrasting them with the polytheists or the wrongdoers. On this basis it is fitting that the emphasis on mentioning these people comes after the conjunctive (law), since the context is to nullify their aim of extinguishing God's light; God's perfecting His light nullifies their aim of extinguishing it. What nullifies the aim of others among the obstinate, namely the polytheists, will come after this.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read (mutimmun nurahu) with tanwin on (mutimmun) and the accusative on (nurahu). Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Khalaf read it without tanwin and with the genitive on (nurihi), taking the active participle as annexed to its object. Both are eloquent.

[Page 192]

﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, even if the polytheists dislike it.﴾

This is an added challenge to the polytheists and their allies among the People of the Book. It reinforces the meaning of His words ﴿And Allah will complete His light, even if the disbelievers dislike it﴾ [al-Saff: 8], and it carries the sense of giving a reason for the sentence that precedes it. The definite form of the two components in His words ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger﴾ conveys a relative restriction (qasr idafi, restriction relative to a specific counter-claim) that refutes the claim of the disbelievers that Muhammad (ﷺ) came on his own initiative. The meaning is: it is Allah, and no other, who sent Muhammad (ﷺ) with guidance and the religion of truth. Likewise, a matter whose accomplishment Allah has undertaken cannot be removed by anyone.

The explanation of this by His words "to make it prevail over all religion" is an announcement that Allah intended the manifestation and spread of this religion, so that they would not hope that it would suffer what the religion of Jesus (peace be upon him) suffered of suppression and weakness at the beginning of its course, and which continued for a long time until Constantine, ruler of the Romans, embraced Christianity. When Allah informed that He intended the manifestation of the religion of Islam over all religions, it became known that its affair continues to grow until the intended purpose is fulfilled.

Al-izhar (the manifestation) means victory, and it is also used for preference and moral elevation.

The definite article in His words "over all religion" (ʿala al-din) is the definite article of the genus (taʿrif al-jins, the definite form denoting the whole class), which implies comprehensiveness (istighraq, inclusion of all members). That is, [Allah will] exalt this true religion over all religions, and grant victory to its adherents over the adherents of other religions who oppose the people of Islam.

It appears that the word "religion" (al-din) is used in both of its meanings: the literal meaning, which is the sacred law (shariʿa), and the figurative meaning, which is its adherents, as when you say: "I entered the village of such-and-such and it honored me." Thus the manifestation of the religion over other religions consists in its being higher than them in legislation and in ethics, and in its being suitable for all people, not specific to one nation over another or to one generation over another.

The manifestation of its adherents over the adherents of other religions consists in granting victory to its adherents over those who oppose them during the period of its manifestation, until its affair is completed and it becomes independent of anyone who supports it.

The promise of Allah has indeed been fulfilled: this religion became manifest, and its adherents came to rule over many nations. Then certain afflictions arose

[Page 193]

from the negligence of the Muslims in establishing the religion in its proper form, so that nations overcame them. As for the religion itself, it has never ceased to be high and witnessed to, by the impartial scholars of the nations, as the best religion for mankind.

The polytheists are singled out for mention here as completing the description of those who dislike the completion of this light and the manifestation of this religion over all religions. It is known that non-polytheists also dislike the manifestation of this religion, because they seek to extinguish the light of the religion; they dislike its manifestation. Thus there occurs in the discourse what is called ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two complementary elements are mentioned, each one omitting what is stated in the other).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 61, verses 10–12:

﴿O you who have believed, shall I direct you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger, and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is best for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿He will forgive you your sins and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. That is the great triumph.﴾

This is a *takhallus* (transition) to the purpose (*gharaḍ*) with which the surah opened, from His saying ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ (Al-Saff: 2) to His saying ﴿as if they were a solid structure﴾ (Al-Saff: 4). After the parables had been presented and the discourse had moved from one domain to another, their address is renewed here in the same manner in which they were addressed at the beginning, with His saying ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ (Al-Saff: 2). That is, "Shall I direct you to the deed most beloved to Allah, so that you may act upon it, just as you asked when you said: 'If we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah, we would act upon them.'" Thus the surah comes in the style of oratory (*khitaba*).

The implied pronoun in (*adullukum*, "I direct you") apparently refers to Allah, the Exalted, because the apparent form of the address is that it is directed from Allah, the Exalted, to the believers. It is also permissible to take the pronoun as referring to the Prophet ﷺ, by supposing an omitted saying (*qawl mahdhuf*). Depending on which interpretation is adopted, the position of His later saying (﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾ (Al-Saff: 13)) differs.

The interrogative is used here for offering (*'ard*) in a figurative sense, because the one who makes an offer may ask the one to whom it is offered in order to learn his desire for the matter being offered, as is said: "Do you have interest in such-and-such?" or "Are you inclined to such-and-such?"

The offering here is a *kināya* (allusion) to arousing eagerness for the matter offered, which is her indicating to them a profitable transaction. The interrogative forms depart from this meaning to many other meanings that are concomitants of the interrogative, as al-Sakkaki noted in *al-Miftah*, and these are not restricted to what he mentioned.

The verb (*adullukum*) is used to convey that what follows is among things that are not easily reached.

The term "transaction" (*tijara*) is applied to righteous deeds by way of *isti'ara* (metaphor), because righteous deeds resemble trade in seeking profit from that deed, in practising it, and in exerting effort in it. This has already been discussed in His saying ﴿so their transaction did not profit﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 16) in Surah al-Baqarah.

Describing the transaction as something that saves from a painful punishment is a *tajrid* (stripping) of the metaphor, for the purpose of making clear this benefit because of its importance. Saving from punishment is not a property of trade; rather, it is one of the appropriate meanings of the literal sense of righteous deeds.

The clause ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*), because the mention of the indication is general, and the arousing of eagerness that preceded it stirs in the hearts of the listeners the question of what this is that You indicate to us and what this transaction is.

Since the address is to a people who are believers, the verb (*tu'minuna billah*, "you believe in Allah") together with (*wa tujahidun*, "and you strive") is intended to mean that you combine belief in Allah and His Messenger with striving in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives, as an elevation of the status of striving. The use of the present tense conveys the command to persist in faith and to renew it at every moment. This is an indirect allusion (*ta'rid*) to the hypocrites and a warning against neglecting the constancy of faith and its requirements.

As for (*tujahidun*, "you strive"), it is for the intention of the renewal of striving whenever they are called forth to it.

The jussive form of (*yaghfir*, "He will forgive") is a warning that (*tu'minuna*, "you believe") and (*wa tujahidun*, "and you strive"), although they come in the form of a statement, mean a command, because the jussive occurs only in the response to a demand, not in the response to a statement. This was said by al-Mubarrad and al-Zamakhshari.

Al-Farra' said: (*yaghfir*) is in the jussive because it is the response to (*hal adullukum*, "shall I direct you"), that is, because the object of (*adullukum*) is the transaction, which is explained as faith and striving. So it is as if it were said: "Will you trade in faith and striving? He will forgive you your sins."

The first two verbs were put in the form of a statement only to signal the obligation of compliance, so that the one commanded imagines that he has heard the command and has complied with it.

The majority (*Jumhur*) read (*tunjikum*, "will save you") with a sukun on the nun and a light jim. Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the nun and a shadda on the jim, as in the expressions *anjahu* and *najjahu* (both meaning "he saved him").

The indication with (*dhalikum*, "that") refers to faith and striving, with the interpretation: "the mentioned thing is best."

The word (*khayr*, "best") here is not the elative form (*ism al-tafdil*) whose original form is *akhyar* and whose pattern is *af'al*. Rather, it is a noun for the opposite of evil, whose pattern is *fa'l*.

His saying (*khayr*) includes what is good in this world and what is good in the Hereafter.

His saying (*in kuntum ta'lamun*, "if you only knew") is an indirect reproach to them for their turning away on the day of Uhud after they had said: "If we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah, we would perform them." They were then summoned to striving, and what happened from them on the day of Uhud occurred, as mentioned at the beginning of the surah. So they were placed in the position of those whose deeds are doubted to be good, because they did not act upon the requirement of knowledge.

The pleasant dwellings (*masakin tayyiba*) are the palaces in Paradise, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and will make for you palaces﴾ (Al-Furqan: 10).

The dwellings are specifically mentioned here because striving involves leaving their dwellings, so they were promised, in recompense for that temporary departure, eternal dwellings. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Say: If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, and your kindred are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 24), up to His saying ﴿and dwellings you are pleased with are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 24), and so on.

That is best for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿He will forgive you your sins and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. The term "transaction" (*tijara*) is applied to righteous deeds by way of *isti'ara* (metaphor), because righteous deeds resemble trade in seeking profit from that deed, in practising it, and in exerting effort in it. Describing the transaction as something that saves from a painful punishment is a *tajrid* (stripping) of the metaphor, for the purpose of making clear this benefit because of its importance. The clause ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (*isti'naf bayani*), because the mention of the indication is general, and the arousing of eagerness that preceded it stirs in the hearts of the listeners the question of what this is that You indicate to us and what this transaction is.

This is an indirect allusion (*ta'rid*) to the hypocrites and a warning against neglecting the constancy of faith and its requirements.

As for (*tujahidun*, "you strive"), it is for the intention of the renewal of striving whenever they are called forth to it.

The jussive form of (*yaghfir*, "He will forgive") is a warning that (*tu'minuna*, "you believe") and (*wa tujahidun*, "and you strive"), although they come in the form of a statement, mean a command, because the jussive occurs only in the response to a demand, not in the response to a statement. This was said by al-Mubarrad and al-Zamakhshari.

Al-Farra' said: (*yaghfir*) is in the jussive because it is the response to (*hal adullukum*, "shall I direct you"), that is, because the object of (*adullukum*) is the transaction, which is explained as faith and striving. So it is as if it were said: "Will you trade in faith and striving? He will forgive you your sins."

The first two verbs were put in the form of a statement only to signal the obligation of compliance, so that the one commanded imagines that he has heard the command and has complied with it.

The majority (*Jumhur*) read (*tunjikum*, "will save you") with a sukun on the nun and a light jim. Ibn 'Amir read it with a fatha on the nun and a shadda on the jim, as in the expressions *anjahu* and *najjahu* (both meaning "he saved him").

The word (*khayr*, "best") here is not the elative form (*ism al-tafdil*) whose original form is *akhyar* and whose pattern is *af'al*. Rather, it is a noun for the opposite of evil, whose pattern is *fa'l*.

His saying (*khayr*) includes what is good in this world and what is good in the Hereafter.

So they were placed in the position of those whose deeds are doubted to be good, because they did not act upon the requirement of knowledge.

It is conjoined to the clause "He will forgive you" and "He will admit you" by ʿaṭf (conjunction of a nominal sentence onto a verbal one). The nominal form was used to convey stability and certainty (thubūt wa-taḥaqquq).

So "ukhrā" (another [favour]) is a mubtada' (subject, topic), whose khabar (predicate) is omitted, indicated by his saying "Shall I direct you" from His saying "He will forgive you." The implied meaning is: "another [favour] for you." It is also permissible to make the khabar his saying "a victory from God."

It is used as a feminine adjective, interpreted as a blessing, a virtue, or a quality, in keeping with what is implied by "He will forgive you your sins" to the end of the verse, in the sense of blessing and quality. This is like His saying, ﴿and another [favour] you were not able to attain﴾ [al-Fath: 21] in Surat al-Fath.

Describing "ukhrā" with the clause "you love" indicates a favour bestowed upon them by giving them what they love in the life of this world before the bestowal of the bliss of the Hereafter. This is similar to His saying, ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah with which you will be pleased﴾ [al-Baqarah: 144].

"A victory from God" is a badal (apposition) to "ukhrā," and it is permissible for it to be a khabar about "ukhrā." What is meant by it is the great victory, which is the victory of the conquest of Makkah, for it was a victory over the fiercest of their enemies, who persecuted and harmed them, expelled them from their homes and their wealth, and incited the Arabs and the confederates against them. They also sought to disfigure their reputation. Added to this was the victory of the religion through the conversion of those who had previously been leaders of disbelief and kindlers of strife, who then became believers and brothers. Mentioning the Name of Majesty (Allah) may be an iẓhār (explicit mention in place of a pronoun) in the position where a pronoun would be expected, on the possibility that the first-person pronoun in His saying "Shall I direct you" is speech from God, the Exalted. It is also permissible for it to follow the apparent requirement of the context if the address was commanded to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), with the implied "Say" (qul).

Describing the conquest as "near" (qarīb) is hastening the joy.

This verse is among the miracles of the Qur'an, which relate to the report of the unseen.

﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾.

It is permissible for this to be a conjunction onto the whole of the speech preceding it, beginning from His saying, ﴿O you who have believed, shall I direct you to a transaction﴾ [al-Saff: 10], on the possibility that what precedes it is speech issuing from God, the Exalted. This is the conjunction of one aim onto another aim, so the command from God to His Prophet (ﷺ) is that he should give good tidings to the believers. In this sentence it is not possible to posit the conjunction of an imperative (inshāʾ) onto a declarative (khabar), since this is not the conjunction of one sentence onto another sentence, but rather of one sentence onto a collection of sentences, in the manner preferred by al-Zamakhsharī in his commentary on His saying, ﴿And give good tidings to those who have believed and done righteous deeds, that they will have gardens﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25] at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah, and by what Sayyid al-Sharīf (al-Jurjānī) explained in his glosses on the Kashshāf.

As for the possibility that His saying, ﴿O you who have believed, shall I direct you﴾ [al-Saff: 10] to the end, is directed toward the command to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to say, ﴿Shall I direct you to a transaction﴾ [al-Saff: 10], with the implied speech "Say," meaning: "Say, O you who have believed, shall I direct you..." to the end, then the imperative in "and give good tidings" is an iltifāt (shift of speaker) of the type tajrīd (a rhetorical device in which the speaker is represented as speaking in his own voice). The meaning is: "And I give good tidings to the believers."

The discussion of the conjunction of an imperative onto a declarative has already preceded, at His saying, ﴿And give good tidings to those who have believed and done righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25], at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

What my opinion has settled upon now is that the difference between the two sentences in being declarative and imperative is a verbal difference which does not affect the connection or disconnection between the two sentences, because connection and disconnection are two semantic matters that follow the aims. Thus the criterion is the semantic relationship, not the verbal form. In this there is sufficiency, since I failed to address this aspect when interpreting the verse in Surat al-Baqarah.

[Page 198]

Here is another address to the believers, completing what was contained in the address beginning with God's words, ﴿O you who believe, shall I guide you to a bargain?﴾ [al-Saff: 10], up to His words, ﴿and strive in the way of God﴾ [al-Saff: 11], which is the purpose of that address. This second address comes as a reminder with a great example from the circumstances of the sincere believers of earlier times, namely the companions of Jesus (peace be upon him), despite their small number and weakness.

God commanded the believers to support the religion. This support is different from the support that is through jihad, because the exhortation to jihad had already been made in His words, ﴿and strive in the way of God with your wealth and your selves﴾ [al-Saff: 11], together with His promise to them that God would grant them victory. So the support commanded here is the support of God's religion, which they believed in, by spreading it and remaining steadfast in holding to it, regardless of the harm they encounter from the polytheists and the People of the Book. God said, ﴿You will surely be tried in your wealth and your selves, and you will surely hear much hurt from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associate others with God. But if you are patient and mindful of God, indeed that is of the matters requiring determination﴾ [Al 'Imran: 186]. This is what was likened to the support of the disciples for the religion of God that Jesus (peace be upon him) brought. Jesus did not wage jihad against those who opposed him, nor were the disciples among those who fought, but he was patient and they were patient, until God made the religion of Christianity prevail and it spread across the earth. Then change crept into it, until Islam came and superseded it from its root.

[Page 199]

*Al-Ansar* (the helpers) is the plural of *nasir*, meaning one who gives strong support.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Abu Ja'far read ﴿kūnū anṣāran lillāh﴾ with tanwin on *anṣāran* and with the lam of attribution before the divine name. In this reading, *anṣāran* is intended to express the sense of the active participle, which indicates occurrence, i.e., "those who bring about support." The lam indicates purpose, i.e., "for the sake of God," meaning "supporters of Him," as He said, ﴿so they have no helper﴾ [Muhammad: 13].

The rest read *anṣāra* with an annexation to the divine name without the lam, considering *Ansar* as a title, in the manner of His words, ﴿who are my helpers﴾.

The comparison with the call of Jesus son of Mary to the disciples and their response is a comparison by way of illustration (*tashbih tamthil*). That is: be, when Muhammad (ﷺ) calls you to support God, like the situation of Jesus son of Mary's words to the disciples and their responding to him.

[Page 200]

The comparison is intended for illustration and emulation, for the disciples fulfilled their promise and remained firm in the religion, and trials and torture did not shake them.

*Ma* is verbal-masdarīya (it turns the following clause into a verbal noun), meaning "like the saying of Jesus and the saying of the disciples." Here an element is omitted, the estimated meaning being "like the case of the saying of Jesus and the saying of the disciples." So the comparison is with both together: Jesus's words and the disciples' response, because the disciples' response is in the position of a statement that follows from Jesus's call. The conjunction *fa* is omitted in such exchanges and dialogues for brevity, as was mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Jesus's words, ﴿Who are my helpers toward God?﴾, are an interrogative to test their readiness to support God's religion with him, similar to the verse of Tarafa:

*When the people say, "Who is a youth?" I think it is I who is meant; I did not grow lazy nor did I become dull.*

The annexation of *anṣār* to the first person pronoun (my) refers to Jesus, in consideration of their being the helpers of his call.

*Ila Allah* (toward God) is connected to *anṣārī* (my helpers). The meaning of *ila* (toward) is figurative terminus (*intiha' majazi*), that is:

[Page 201]

turning toward God. Their calling people to the religion and teaching them what God is pleased with for them is likened to the striving of those who strive toward God to help Him, as one who seeks aid goes to the place of those whom he seeks aid from so they may help him against one who has overcome him.

So in the particle *ila* there is a subsidiary metaphor (*isti'ara taba'iyya*). For this reason, the response reported from the disciples corresponds to the interrogative, when they said, "We are the helpers of God," meaning: we support God against those who oppose Him and act hostilely toward Him, that is, we support His religion.

*Al-Hawariyyun* (the disciples) is the plural of *hawari*, with a fatha on the ha and a light waw, and it is a word arabicized from the Abyssinian (*Habashiyya*) *hawariya*, meaning the devoted companion. It is not Arabic in origin nor derived from an Arabic root. Al-Dahhak counted it among the arabicized words, but he said it is Nabataean. The meaning of *hawari* is "launderer," as in *al-Itqan*.

*Al-Hawariyyun* is a name the Qur'an gave to the twelve companions of Jesus. There is no doubt that it was known among the Arab Christians, who took it from the Christians of Abyssinia. This name is not found in the Gospels.

[Page 202]

The Prophet (ﷺ) named al-Zubayr ibn al-'Awwam his *hawari*, by way of likening him to one of the disciples, and he said, "Every prophet has a disciple, and my disciple is al-Zubayr." The mention of the disciples has already occurred in His words, ﴿The disciples said, "We are the helpers of God"﴾ in Surat Al 'Imran.

Know that the statement of Jesus (peace be upon him) reported in this verse is not the statement reported in the verse of Al 'Imran, for that one was directed at the group of the Children of Israel, from whom he sensed disbelief when he called them to belief in him.

As for his statement reported here, it is directed to those who believed in him, asking them for their support, according to His words, ﴿as Jesus son of Mary said to the disciples﴾, etc. Therefore it is necessary that the requirements of the two similar statements differ. According to the difference of the two contexts, the consideration of the specific features in the two statements also differs, even if they are similar. There we took the annexation of "helpers of God" as a verbal annexation (*idafa lafziyya*), and thus the disciples' statement, ﴿We are the helpers of God﴾, did not convey restriction (*qasr*) because the predicate was not definite. Here, however, it is more apparent that the phrase "helpers of God" was taken as a title for the disciples, by which they identified themselves and which they bestowed upon themselves. Therefore they wished to use it as evidence that they are the most worthy of people of realizing its meaning. Accordingly, the annexation of *anṣār* to the divine name here is a semantic annexation (*idafa ma'nawiyya*), conveying definiteness. Thus the sentence ﴿We are the helpers of God﴾ here includes a form of restriction, unlike its counterpart in Surat Al 'Imran.

So in the report of the disciples' response here there is the specific feature of the form of restriction through the definiteness of the subject and predicate, and the specific feature of definiteness through annexation. Thus it is a concise report of their response: they answered by committing themselves to supporting the Messenger, and by making themselves deserving of this support, because they devoted themselves wholly to supporting the religion and became known for it, and by confining the support of the religion to themselves with a restriction that conveys emphasis on their complete devotion to it, as if there were no supporter of the religion besides them, despite their small number. It also implicitly indicates the disbelief of the rest of their people from the Children of Israel.

After the disciples' statement, "We are the helpers," there follows the report that the Children of Israel split into two groups: one group believed in Jesus and what he brought, and another group disbelieved in that. This sequential linking (*tafri'*) requires an implied statement, which is: "So they supported God by calling to Him and persevering in it. Some of the Children of Israel responded, and some disbelieved." Only a small number of the Children of Israel responded to them, for the Gospel of Luke reports that the followers of Jesus were more than seventy.

The purpose of His words, ﴿A group of the Children of Israel believed and a group disbelieved﴾, is to prepare for His words, ﴿So We strengthened those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant﴾. *Ta'yid* (strengthening), *nasr* (support) and *taqwiya* (empowerment) are synonyms. God strengthened the people of Christianity with many of those who followed Christianity through the call of the disciples and their followers, such as Paul.

He said, ﴿So We strengthened those who believed﴾ and did not say "so We strengthened them," because the strengthening was for the collective of those who believed in Jesus, not for each individual among them, since a great number of his followers were killed, mutilated, and thrown to wild beasts in public gatherings to be torn apart. Among the disciples who were killed was the chief disciple whom Jesus named Peter, meaning "the rock," for his steadfastness in God.

They claim that his body is in the great church in Rome known as the Church of Saint Peter. Judging the collective in such a case is common, as you say, "God granted victory to the Muslims at Badr," even though some of them were killed. The intended meaning is the support of the religion.

The purpose of this report is the promise to the Muslims who were commanded to be the helpers of God, that God will strengthen them against their enemy.

The word *'aduww* (enemy) is applied to the singular and the plural. God said, ﴿and they are an enemy to you﴾ [al-Kahf: 50], and it was discussed earlier at His words, ﴿O you who believe, do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1] in Surat al-Mumtahanah.

*Al-zahir* is the victorious, the dominant. It is said *zahara 'alayhi*, meaning he overcame him, and *zahara bihi*, meaning he overcame by means of him, i.e., with his help. The root of the verb is derived from the non-derived noun *zahr*, which is the central spine of the human body and animals, because the strength of an animal lies in the back. This is like the verb *'adada* derived from *'adud* (upper arm). And *ayyada* is derived from *yad* (hand). Among its inflections are *zaahara 'alayhi* (backed him), *istazhara* (sought help), and *zahir lahu* (supporter of him). He said, ﴿and the angels after that are a supporter﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. So the meaning of *zahirin* (dominant) is that they were victorious, because the outcome of victory belonged to them, and they were empowered to rule over the Jews who disbelieved in Jesus, and they tore them to pieces, every tearing.
